nodes.content: Enable identifiable species-removal predictions from compositional microbial time series despite environmental confounding and sparse absolute-abundance measurements.
requirements: Specify sufficient identifiability assumptions and characterize observationally indistinguishable communities with different removal responses.
Reduce held-out post-removal log-abundance RMSE by 20% versus generalized Lotka–Volterra models using identical observations.

nodes.content: Develop an environment-adjusted, biomass-anchored state-space model with intervention-invariant dynamics, observability tests, and indistinguishable-community counterexamples for species-removal forecasts.
Which environmental-forcing symmetries survive weekly biomass anchors and yield identical observational trajectories but divergent species-removal responses?
When unmeasured forcing tracks species abundance, trading environmental coefficients for interaction coefficients preserves anchored trajectories but changes removal forecasts.
Construct forcing–interaction swaps under weekly biomass anchors, derive observability rank conditions, and compare paired species-removal forecasts.
Simulate 100 six-taxon compositional series with abundance-correlated forcing and weekly biomass anchors; test swapped models’ observational equivalence and removal divergence.
Across 100 simulations, swapped models matched compositions and biomass within 0.01 log units; median removal divergence was 0.8 log units.
Require measured forcing and full-rank abundance–environment excitation for point forecasts; report removal-response bounds when these fail.
Package the six-taxon swap benchmark with 100 paired trajectories, weekly biomass anchors, matched observational fits, and divergent removal forecasts.
Augment six-taxon swap benchmark with independently varying measured forcing; compare observability-gated forecasts against identical-input gLV using held-out removal log-abundance RMSE.
On held-out six-taxon removals, observability-gated RMSE was 0.64 versus identical-input gLV’s 0.69 log units, only 7% lower.
Zero-integral shared environmental pulses between weekly anchors preserve observed compositions and biomass yet alter density-dependent removal responses.
Inject zero-integral common-forcing pulses between weekly biomass anchors in six-taxon simulations; quantify compositional mismatch and removal-response divergence.
Across 100 simulations, pulse pairs matched CLR and biomass within 0.01 log units; median removal divergence reached 0.42 log units.
Combine randomized environmental-pulse controls with targeted biomass anchors and equivalence-class-aware removal forecasts, using identical observations for gLV.
Derive rank conditions and equivalence bounds under randomized forcing and timed anchors; target 20% held-out RMSE reduction versus matched-input gLV.
Extend the six-taxon swap benchmark with randomized pulse schedules and midweek biomass anchors; compute observability ranks and removal-equivalence bounds.
Release PulseAnchor-6 with randomized forcing schedules, midweek biomass anchors, observability-rank labels, and paired removal-response bounds.
Benchmark both proposals against identical-input gLV on PulseAnchor-6 held-out removals, stratifying log-abundance RMSE and bound coverage by rank.
PulseAnchor-6 full-rank removal RMSEs: p2 0.52, p1 0.66, gLV 0.69 log units; rank-deficient bounds covered 94%.
Does p2 retain a 20% overall removal-RMSE advantage when pulse timing is uncertain or midweek biomass anchors are missing?
With ≤12-hour pulse-timing jitter and 10% missing midweek anchors, p2 retains ≥20% overall removal-RMSE reduction versus identical-input gLV.
Perturb PulseAnchor-6 with ±12-hour pulse-timing jitter and 10% missing midweek anchors; compare overall held-out removal RMSE against identical-input gLV.
With ±12-hour jitter and 10% missing anchors, overall removal RMSE was 0.57 versus gLV’s 0.73 log units (22% lower).
Run 500 independently parameterized PulseAnchor-6 replicates with ±12-hour jitter and 10% missing anchors; bootstrap p2’s removal-RMSE improvement over identical-input gLV.
Across 500 replicates, p2 averaged 0.62 versus gLV’s 0.73 log-unit RMSE (15% lower); 95% bootstrap improvement interval: 12–18%.
Marginalizing pulse timing and missing-anchor biomass states, rather than using plug-in estimates, restores ≥20% average removal-RMSE improvement across independent replicates.
Refit 500 PulseAnchor-6 jitter/dropout replicates, marginalizing pulse times and missing biomass; bootstrap removal-RMSE gains versus identical-input gLV.
Across 500 replicates, marginalized p2 achieved 0.56 versus gLV’s 0.73 log-unit removal RMSE (23% lower; 95% bootstrap gain: 21–26%).
Predict removals using randomized taxon-specific knockdowns, biomass spike-ins, and latent-environment controls; certify identifiability or bound ambiguous responses.
What knockdown specificity and biomass spike-in frequency break interaction–environment symmetries when environmental feedback remains unmeasured?
Under linear, invariant shared environmental feedback, ≥95%-specific randomized knockdowns and twice-weekly biomass spike-ins identify six-taxon removal responses.
Derive knockdown observability conditions; simulate six-taxon feedback across 90–100% specificity and weekly versus twice-weekly spike-ins; validate removal forecasts.
Extend PulseAnchor-6 with 90–100%-specific knockdowns and linear feedback; test weekly/twice-weekly spike-in observability and marginalized-p2 removal RMSE versus identical-input gLV.
Across 500 runs, ≥95%-specific knockdowns and twice-weekly spike-ins yielded full-rank observability; marginalized p2 RMSE was 0.55 versus gLV’s 0.73.
Release KnockdownAnchor-6 with specificity sweeps, weekly/twice-weekly spike-ins, feedback parameters, observability ranks, and matched-input gLV benchmarks.
Extend KnockdownAnchor-6 with nonlinear feedback and intervention-induced environmental shifts; test p3 identifiability certificates and removal RMSE against matched-input gLV.
Across 500 nonlinear-feedback runs, p3 flagged 92% of shift-induced ambiguities; certified removals achieved 0.54 versus gLV’s 0.72 log-unit RMSE.
Stress-test KnockdownAnchor-6 with 85–95% knockdown specificity and latent feedback shifts; measure false identifiability certificates and held-out removal RMSE.
Across 500 low-specificity runs, p3 falsely certified 31% of ambiguous removals; RMSE was 0.69 versus gLV’s 0.72 log units.
Can measured off-target effects and sham knockdowns restore valid identifiability certificates and ≥20% RMSE gains at 85–95% specificity?
At 85–95% specificity, off-target calibration and sham controls yield <5% false certificates and ≥20% removal-RMSE reduction versus matched-input gLV.
Calibrate off-target effects with sham knockdowns in 500 low-specificity KnockdownAnchor-6 runs; compare false-certificate rates and matched-input gLV removal RMSE.
Across 500 calibrated runs, false certificates fell to 4%; removal RMSE was 0.56 versus matched-input gLV’s 0.72 log units.
Adopt calibrated p3 only with measured off-target effects and sham controls; otherwise report response bounds, not point-identified removal forecasts.
Fit sentinel-adjusted hierarchical state-space dynamics using noninteracting strains and taxon-specific qPCR anchors across replicate communities for removal forecasts.
Derive sentinel/qPCR observability conditions, construct indistinguishable removal pairs, and target ≥20% held-out RMSE reduction versus identical-input gLV.
Adapt PulseAnchor-6 using n40-calibrated off-target controls, two noninteracting sentinel strains, and weekly taxon-specific qPCR; test observability rank and removal RMSE.
Release SentinelAnchor-6 with sentinel trajectories, weekly taxon-specific qPCR, calibrated off-target controls, observability labels, and matched-input gLV splits.
Audit SentinelAnchor-6 observability labels against indistinguishable pairs; benchmark sentinel-adjusted forecasts versus identical-input gLV on held-out removal RMSE.
On 300 full-rank SentinelAnchor-6 removals, p4 RMSE was 0.49 versus gLV’s 0.65 log units; ambiguity labels matched constructed pairs.
Stress-test SentinelAnchor-6 with weak sentinel cross-feeding and 30% missing qPCR; measure false identifiability certificates and matched-input gLV removal RMSE.
Under cross-feeding and 30% missing qPCR, false certificates reached 23%; removal RMSE was 0.64 versus matched-input gLV’s 0.68.
Can sentinel cross-feeding calibration and adaptively timed qPCR restore valid certificates and ≥20% removal-RMSE gains under 30% missing measurements?
Calibrating sentinel cross-feeding and scheduling qPCR at predicted rank bottlenecks lowers false certificates below 5% and removal RMSE by ≥20%.
Calibrate sentinel cross-feeding and schedule qPCR at rank bottlenecks in 30%-missing SentinelAnchor-6; compare false certificates and matched-input gLV RMSE.
Across 300 calibrated SentinelAnchor-6 removals, false certificates were 8%; RMSE was 0.56 versus matched-input gLV’s 0.68 log units (18% lower).
Uncertainty-aware cross-feeding models and worst-case qPCR scheduling yield <5% false certificates and ≥20% RMSE reduction versus matched-input gLV.
On 300 30%-missing SentinelAnchor-6 runs, fit uncertainty-aware cross-feeding and worst-case qPCR scheduling; benchmark false certificates and matched-input gLV RMSE.
Across 300 runs, uncertainty-aware calibration produced 3% false certificates; RMSE was 0.53 versus matched-input gLV’s 0.68 (22% lower).
Adopt uncertainty-aware cross-feeding calibration and worst-case qPCR scheduling for p4: 3% false certificates, 22% RMSE gain; otherwise bound removals.
